Sign your commits with Secretive (preferred) or 1Password. Signing proves you authored them, since the Author field can be forged [1]. Secretive steps [2]:
1. Create a new key in Secretive and name it "Git signing key", with Protection Level set to Notify.
2. Go to Integrations, click Git Signing, and pick that key.
3. Paste the ~/.gitconfig and ~/.gitallowedsigners snippets into those files. If ~/.gitconfig already has content, merge the new sections in.
4. Set SSH_AUTH_SOCK for your shell as Secretive instructs.
5. Copy your public key. The signingkey in ~/.gitconfig points to a file, so run `cat <path-from-signingkey> | pbcopy`.
6. In your GitHub SSH keys settings, add it as a Signing Key.
7. Test with `git commit --allow-empty -m "test signing"`, push, and check for a green Verified badge.

For 1Password, follow its git commit signing guide [3]. Afterwards, turn on "Flag unsigned commits as unverified" in your GitHub profile [4].

Refunds are covered by the sales refunds page. Support reviews requests and issues refunds or credits, and escalates unusual or large ones to RevOps.

**Eligibility.** The request must come within 30 days of the billing date, with a reasonable explanation that fits one of the scenarios. The account must show no fraud or abuse. For volume spikes, the unusual usage must have stopped and the customer must have taken steps such as setting a billing limit [1]. The scenarios are learning curve, unexpected stardom, under attack (bot spikes) and wrong setup [2].

**Repeat incidents.** The first incident follows the standard policy. After that, refunds depend on whether the customer acted on our earlier advice. Partial refunds of up to 50% are possible while they fix the problem [3].

**Channels.** In-app tickets go to the Support team, who review the request and issue the refund or credit [4].

**Calculating the amount.** Work out the customer's normal usage, then price the baseline and the baseline plus overage. The refund is the difference. Don't price the overage amount alone, because of tiered pricing [5].

**Credit or refund.** If the customer's period hasn't ended and the invoice isn't finalized, issue credits. If the invoice is finalized and this is a first request, refund through a credit note, not the refund button [6].

**Escalate to RevOps** for big customers ($1,667+ monthly), multiple recent refunds, cases that don't fit the simple scenarios, or anything needing an invoice created or changed. Support shouldn't create or modify invoices [7].

Re-run the missing day's report with a Django management command from a production pod. Usage reports run daily at midnight BST and are normally generated in posthog/posthog [1]. When the cron is interrupted, the billing service doesn't receive any reports, and usage isn't sent to Stripe [1].

**Spotting it:** the Metabase Revenue dashboard shows fewer reports than usual, with one instance (generally US) at 0. The Growth dashboard's Usage report insight shows a big dip [1].

**Re-running it:** connect to PostHog Cloud infra first, then run `python manage.py send_usage_report --date YYYY-MM-DD --async 1` [1]. The date is one day after the day with missing reports, because reports cover the previous day's usage. If May 11 had 0 reports, use May 12 [1]. Async is recommended so you don't wait on the billing requests, but afterwards check that it completed with no errors or ClickHouse timeouts [1]. Without async, an interrupted run fails with exit code 137, so reconnect and retry [1].

**Getting onto the infra:** first get AWS access, and follow the whole guide [2]. Then, once you have EKS cluster access and are on the internal network, list pods with `kubectl -n posthog get pods` (you'll most likely want a web pod). Open a shell with `kubectl -n posthog exec --stdin --tty <POD_NAME> -- /bin/bash` [2]. Run the command above from that shell.

Before you agree, check two things.

A month only counts as a spike if all three conditions hold. Revenue must be more than twice the average of the previous two months. The increase must be at least $1000. Top-line reporting is different. Unadjusted revenue is still used for top-line and overall growth metrics [6].

Chase it yourself, following the late-payment steps. Overdue invoices can also cost you commission.

**What counts as late:** For credit-based customers, it's an unpaid invoice past its due date, usually Net 30 from the contract start. This applies even if credits remain [1].

**What to do:** The account owner in Vitally owns this. If there's no owner, Simon handles it [1]. The steps are:
1. Day it becomes late: you get a Vitally risk indicator and a #sales-alerts tag. Contact known contacts and the finance emails in Stripe. Include the invoice PDF, and say access will be suspended if payment doesn't arrive within 7 calendar days [2].
2. One day before suspension: contact all active users on the account [3].
3. Suspend access: set the org's "Active" field to "No" in the Django admin panel, then tell all users [4].
4. One day before cancelling: warn all contacts that the subscription will be terminated [5].
5. Cancel the subscription in Stripe [6].

**Commission:** Commission is paid quarterly and is subject to clawbacks if invoices remain unpaid [7]. Overdue invoices from the current quarter are excluded from the payout. The cutoff is the 14th of the month after quarter end [8]. If an invoice is issued late in the quarter but due after that cutoff, you're paid on good faith. If it later becomes overdue, it is clawed back in that quarter [9]. The handbook tells AEs not to hand invoice-chasing to a finance person [10].
